q: To overthrow his former opinions, Descartes says he doesn't need to prove each one false. Instead he will:
a: Reject any opinion in which he finds any occasion for doubt, by attacking their foundations
w: Examine every belief one by one
Accept only beliefs approved by the Church
Keep beliefs that most people share
e: Once the foundation (the senses) is undermined, everything built on it falls 'of its own accord'.

q: What is the main source Descartes says all his previously accepted 'truths' came from?
e: 'Whatever I have hitherto admitted as most true, that I received either from, or by my Senses', and the senses sometimes deceive.

q: Descartes' response to 'surely I can't doubt I'm sitting by the fire in my winter gown' is:
a: He has often dreamed exactly such things while lying in bed
w: He might be a brain in a vat
e: The dreaming argument: there are no sure signs to distinguish waking from sleep.

q: Descartes uses the analogy of painters inventing mermaids and satyrs to argue that even dream images are built from:
a: Simpler, more universal things (extension, shape, quantity, number, place, time)
e: Even a wholly invented picture uses real colors. Likewise dreams are composed of simple, general things.

q: After the dreaming argument, which sciences does Descartes initially think still contain something certain?
e: 'Whether I sleep or wake, two and three added make five.' Sciences of composite things (physics, astronomy, medicine) are doubtful.

q: What possibility makes Descartes doubt even that 2 + 3 = 5?
a: An omnipotent God (or deceiver) could make him err whenever he adds
e: The dreaming argument leaves math intact. The deceiver hypothesis extends doubt to math too.

q: Descartes compares his tendency to slip back into old opinions to:
a: A prisoner who dreams of liberty and is afraid to wake
e: He willingly falls back into comfortable opinions, fearing the toilsome waking of doubt.

q: Descartes begins Meditation II feeling as though he has:
a: Fallen into a deep whirlpool/gulf where he can neither touch bottom nor swim to the top
e: Yesterday's doubts left him 'plunged on a sudden into a deep gulf'.

a: Needed only one firm, immovable point to move the whole Earth
w: Doubted the existence of the external world
e: Likewise, Descartes needs just one certain, indisputable truth.

q: In Meditation II, 'I am, I exist' is necessarily true:
a: Whenever it is spoken or thought by me
w: Only when I perceive my body
At all times, whether or not I think
e: Even if the deceiver deceives me, I must exist to be deceived. The certainty holds 'whilst I think that I am'.

q: Which faculty does Descartes find cannot be separated from himself?
e: Nutrition and motion need a body, and sensing happens in dreams too. 'Thought, this alone cannot be separated from me.'

q: Descartes concludes he is 'only a thinking thing'. Which of these does he include in thinking?
a: Doubting, understanding, affirming, denying, willing, imagining, and sensing
e: A thinking thing doubts, understands, affirms, denies, wills, refuses, imagines and perceives.

q: Why does Descartes say he can't use imagination to learn what he is?
a: To imagine is to contemplate the image of a corporeal thing, and bodies are still in doubt
e: Using imagination to know the self would be like falling asleep to see something more clearly in a dream.

q: In the wax example, after the wax is melted by the fire, what remains of the wax?
a: Only something extended, flexible, and changeable
e: Every sensory quality changed, yet it's the same wax. So what we know of it isn't given by the senses.

q: The wax example concludes that we know bodies through:
a: The inspection of the mind (understanding) alone
e: Imagination can't run through the wax's innumerable possible changes. Only the understanding grasps what the wax is.

q: Descartes looks out the window and 'sees' men in the street, though he only sees hats and coats that could cover automata. The point is:
a: What we think we see with the eyes, we actually judge with the mind
e: He judges them to be men by his 'judicative faculty', not by sight alone.

q: What is the final conclusion of Meditation II?
a: Nothing can be perceived more easily or evidently than one's own mind
w: The body is better known than the mind
The external world is an illusion
e: Every act of perceiving the wax gives even more evidence of the mind doing the perceiving.
